meta.title: Use and Maintenance of Herbarium Cabinet in Pharmacognosy Laboratory

sections.purpose: To safely store, organize, and preserve authenticated herbarium voucher specimens of medicinal plants and crude drug samples for long-term reference, teaching, and pharmacognostic authentication.
sections.scope: Applicable to Pharmacognosy laboratory herbarium for permanent storage of authenticated plant specimens used as reference standards for crude drug identification.
procedure: Ensure the herbarium cabinet is clean, dry, and free of insects before placing new specimens.
Fumigate the cabinet quarterly using paradichlorobenzene (naphthalene) crystals or thymol to prevent insect damage — place fumigant in small cloth bags in the top corners of each drawer.
Organize herbarium sheets alphabetically by family and genus-species name within each drawer.
Assign a unique accession number to each mounted herbarium sheet before filing.
Place a printed herbarium label firmly on each sheet: botanical name, family, local name, collection number, date, location, collector name, and determiner name.
File sheets horizontally in drawers — do not overfill drawers (maximum 5–8 cm height of sheets per drawer).
Place a separator card (Kraft paper) between each species to prevent abrasion between mounted specimens.
Insert a 'POISON' label inside drawers containing specimens of toxic plants.
Keep a cross-reference index register: accession number, botanical name, family, collection date, and drawer/row location.
Check specimens every 6 months for: insect damage (holes, frass), mould (white powdery growth), label deterioration, and mounting paper damage.
Repair damaged mounting paper and reattach loose specimens immediately using archival PVA glue.
Replace deteriorated labels with new printed labels maintaining all original data.
Record all additions, withdrawals, and condition checks in the herbarium register.
Restrict access to authorized personnel only — log all specimen withdrawals for study or comparison.
precautions: Never allow food or drinks near the herbarium — food attracts insects.
Maintain relative humidity between 45–55% and temperature between 15–20°C — high humidity causes mould; high temperature causes brittleness.
Install a data-logging hygrometer inside the cabinet to continuously monitor humidity.
Do not store fresh or incompletely dried specimens — moisture causes mould that destroys adjacent specimens.
Handle dried herbarium specimens with extreme care — they are very brittle.
Fumigate new incoming specimens for 2 weeks in an isolation area before adding to the main collection.
Keep the cabinet tightly closed when not in use to exclude insects and dust.
Do not expose herbarium specimens to direct sunlight — UV causes rapid fading of colours and deterioration of paper.
